introduction: Today's feast of the Baptism of the Lord brings the Christmas season to a close. As Jesus comes up out of the waters of the Jordan, the heavens are torn open, the Spirit descends like a dove, and the Father's voice declares, "You are my beloved Son." Isaiah invites all who thirst to come to the waters. As we celebrate, let us give thanks for our own baptism and renew our desire to live as God's beloved children.

prayerOfTheFaithful.invitation: Through baptism we have become children of God. With confidence, let us pray to our Father.
intentions: For the Church: that all the baptised may live as beloved sons and daughters of God and witnesses to his love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those preparing for baptism, and for parents and godparents: that they may receive the gift of new life with faith and joy. Let us pray to the Lord.
For all who thirst, for water, for justice or for meaning: that God may satisfy them, and that we may help. Let us pray to the Lord.
For those who have forgotten their baptism or drifted from the Church: that they may hear again the Father's voice of love. Let us pray to the Lord.
For our parish: that as Christmas ends we may begin Ordinary Time renewed in our baptismal promises. Let us pray to the Lord.
prayerOfTheFaithful.conclusion: Father, at the Jordan you declared Jesus your beloved Son and anointed him with the Holy Spirit. Hear our prayers, and keep us faithful to our baptism. Through Christ our Lord.

reflection.title: The heavens torn open
reflection.body:
On the First Sunday of Advent, Isaiah prayed: "Oh that you would tear the heavens, that you would come down." Today, at the end of the Christmas season, Mark tells us that prayer has been answered. As Jesus comes up out of the water, "he saw the heavens parting and the Spirit descending on him like a dove." The word Mark uses for "parting" is the word for tearing. The heavens have been torn open. God has come down.

Then the Father speaks: "You are my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased." Before Jesus has preached a sermon or worked a miracle, the Father declares his love and delight in him. His mission begins from that certainty.

Why was Jesus baptised at all? John's baptism was for sinners, and Jesus had no sin. The Church's answer is that he stepped into the water to stand with us, taking his place among sinners at the very beginning of his ministry. He did not need the water to make him holy; he made the water holy for us.

That is why today is also about our own baptism. In baptism we were united to Christ. The Father now says to each of us what he said at the Jordan: you are my beloved child. We did not earn it; it was given. Everything else in the Christian life (our prayer, our service, our struggles against sin) flows from that gift.

Isaiah's invitation fits this feast beautifully: "Come, everyone who thirsts, to the waters! Come, he who has no money, buy, and eat!" God's grace is free. And God's word, like rain that waters the earth, "will not return to me void, but it will accomplish that which I please."

This week, we might find out the date of our baptism and celebrate it, or renew our baptismal promises in prayer. As Ordinary Time begins, let us live as beloved children of the Father.
